lesson.title: Old Hickory: The General Who Became President
lesson.summary: A frontier born war hero turned populist president, Andrew Jackson expanded executive power and democratic participation for white men while inflicting devastating harm on Native nations.
lesson.body:
Andrew Jackson was born in 1767 in the Waxhaws region along the border of North and South Carolina, into a Scots Irish frontier family, and he rose from a hardscrabble, orphaned childhood to become one of the most consequential and polarizing figures in American history. He first became a national hero through his military career, most famously commanding the decisive American victory at the Battle of New Orleans in January 1815 during the War of 1812, a win that made him instantly famous even though it came after the peace treaty had already been signed.

Jackson's military reputation also rested on brutal campaigns against Native nations. During the Creek War, he led American forces to a crushing victory over the Red Stick faction of the Creek Nation at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend in 1814, a defeat that forced the Creek to cede tens of millions of acres of land in Georgia and Alabama. A few years later, during the First Seminole War of 1817 and 1818, Jackson invaded Spanish Florida without clear authorization, seizing Spanish forts and executing two British subjects, actions that stirred controversy but also helped pressure Spain into ceding Florida to the United States in 1821.

After losing the contested election of 1824 to John Quincy Adams despite winning the most popular and electoral votes, an outcome Jackson's supporters branded a corrupt bargain, Jackson built the political coalition that became the Democratic Party and won the presidency decisively in 1828. His inauguration in March 1829 became famous for the crowds of ordinary citizens who poured into the White House to celebrate, a scene that supporters saw as democracy in action and critics saw as mob rule. Jackson cultivated an image as a rough hewn man of the people, though in reality he was a wealthy slaveholding planter who owned the Hermitage, a large cotton plantation near Nashville, Tennessee.

As president from 1829 to 1837, Jackson expanded the power of the executive branch more aggressively than any predecessor, using the veto far more often than earlier presidents and treating himself as the direct representative of the American people rather than merely an officer of Congress. His two terms were defined by several major confrontations: his long fight against the Second Bank of the United States, which he vetoed and ultimately defunded, his forceful response to South Carolina's attempt at nullification in 1832 and 1833, and his aggressive implementation of Indian removal policy in the Southeast, which led directly to the suffering later remembered as the Trail of Tears.

Jackson's legacy remains sharply contested. He is remembered as a champion of expanded democracy for white men and as a forceful defender of the Union against nullification, yet his presidency also brought the forced displacement of tens of thousands of Native Americans and rested on a political appeal that offered greater freedom to some Americans while denying it entirely to others. His face later appeared on the twenty dollar bill, and historians continue to debate how to weigh his democratic legacy against the human cost of his policies.
